item.title: Peering Into the Privacy of Smart Glasses
item.dc:creator: Rina Diane Caballar
item.description: Researchers, providers, and consumers are keeping a close eye on the devices' surveillance features.
item.content:encoded:
Smart glasses are making a spectacle.

These AI-augmented devices can see, hear, and understand your surroundings, answering questions, dictating directions, and translating conversations. For people who are blind or have low vision, smart glasses can prove transformative,a helping them navigate their surroundings and complete certain tasks on their own.

Yet the wearable tech also puts privacy risks in plain view. Reports have surfaced of people using camera-equipped eyewear to surreptitiously film those around them,b later posting the recorded footage on social media.c Some videos might even be fed to AI models for training and, in some cases, may be subject to human review.

“The amount of data that these smart glasses are collecting is a lot more than people probably realize,” said Milica Stilinovic, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Sydney in Australia who focuses on technological harms and the governance of emerging technologies. She raised additional concerns around how data is stored and used, as well as questionable data retention practices.

Glimpses of Privacy

Some companies are attempting to solve these issues. HTC’s Vive Eagle glasses,d for instance, won’t record unless they’re physically worn, and people nearby can say “stop recording” to instantly end the footage. Others have removed cameras altogether, such as Mira’s AI glasses,e which only keep transcripts without recording or storing audio.

However, Stilinovic regards these as “stopgap measures aiming to address the market in a way that doesn’t essentially eradicate the problem.”

A more apt solution entails wearable tech creators integrating privacy from the start, according to Lorrie Cranor, director and Bosch Distinguished Professor of the CyLab Security and Privacy Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. “They should put privacy front and center in the design process,” said Cranor, who’s also an ACM fellow and a member of the ACM CHI Academy.

Privacy by design acts as a guiding principle for Raven Resonance. The startup is crafting Raven Prism, which founder Thomas Suarez likens to “a full computer on your face” that can be controlled using your eyes and voice. He envisions a spatial future where instead of displaying apps on a screen, they exist as 3D objects “that are ambient around you, and they’re just there when you need them and gone when you don’t.”

Raven Prism, which is set to launch this fall, incorporates privacy features that blend restriction with indication: a colored physical camera cover that must be manually swiveled up, a bright red ring around the camera, and “Beakon” lights (named after a bird’s beak, in keeping with the bird theme) around the frame’s bottom rims that fade in and out in certain colors depending on whether the camera or microphone is turned on. Wearers can run small AI models locally, Suarez said, and since processing happens on-device, data stays on-device too.

“Smart glasses have more sensors and radios that can peer into people’s private lives than any personal computing device in history,” wrote Suarez in a postf detailing the team’s design decisions. “This is a major responsibility for anyone building in the wearable computing space. Our team is strongly against having any part in the creation of a device that promotes surveillance.”

Safeguards in Sight

With smart glasses, there’s more to privacy than meets the eye. It needs to be weaved into what the wearables sense, compute, retain, and communicate to those around them, said Faraz Faruqi, a recent Ph.D. graduate at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory whose research focused on human-computer interaction, generative AI, and interactive systems.

“Designers can ask what information a feature actually needs,” Faruqi said. “Not every capability requires a high-resolution image; depth, infrared, lower-resolution imaging, or other sensing modalities may sometimes provide enough information while capturing less identity-rich data.”

Raw sensor data can be processed within a constrained environment on the device and can be ephemeral rather than automatically stored, Faruqi suggested. Citing navigation as an example, he noted that a device might say “there’s a step ahead” by inferring information from the captured street image or video instead of directly accessing the underlying camera feed and without retaining the image or video.

Stilinovic recommends additional protective methods, such as blurring the faces of bystanders, opt-out mechanisms for collecting data, and stronger oversight. “We need to have particular regulatory measures that address the contemporary realities of this tech,” she added, including updating our understanding of privacy and consent in the era of AI glasses.

For Cranor, participatory designg of both wearers and nonwearers remains vital, considering helpful use cases and the least amount of information required to fulfill them. “We need to have a framework for what is acceptable, what is not acceptable, and how to minimize the unnecessary recording and action on data that’s beyond the use case.”

Faruqi echoed the sentiment: “A better goal is to design glasses that collect only the sensory information they need, process more of it locally, retain less of it, and communicate clearly to both wearers and bystanders what they are doing. Privacy therefore also means making sensing and recording legible to bystanders and thinking about what meaningful agency they can have when they are being sensed by someone else’s device.”

A Blurry Outlook

Looking to the future, Stilinovic doubts smart glasses will become a fixture in our everyday lives. “Currently, the harms are outweighing the benefits,” she observed.

The backlash seems to be growing, with consumer venues introducing policies to restrict the technology, countries weighing bans in government workplaces and public spaces, and courts and schools barring their use. Some retailers have even halted salesh of Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses.

“I know we’ve heard from tech companies that smart glasses will be the natural extension of the human experience,” Stilinovic said, “but unless those privacy issues are addressed, I don’t see them being of benefit in the future.”

Cranor, on the other hand, hopes “We don’t have to go to the extreme of just banning smart glasses. I don’t think it’s all or nothing; I think we need to figure out how we can have them without them being complete tools of surveillance.”

The potential ubiquity of smart glasses, Faraz said, will depend on “how we develop technical safeguards and social norms that make people around them comfortable with their presence.” With today’s smartphones, for instance, raising them to take a photo or video is a visible and recognizable signal. But for smart glasses, “many of those cues are different,” he said, “so new technical mechanisms and social norms will have to develop alongside the technology.”

item.title: When Espionage is Outsourced
item.dc:creator: David Geer
item.description: Recurring artifacts across unrelated sectors distinguish commercial espionage platforms from bespoke pipelines and reveal a centralized infrastructure serving multiple state clients.
item.content:encoded:
When nation-states rely on private offensive vendors to attack infrastructure, cyber espionage operates under a state-enablement model. Instead of engineering custom tools per operation, state actors consume managed relay networks and automated scanning suites from shared vendors. This model speeds perimeter probing across global targets while masking the origins of attacks behind compromised consumer hardware.

On August 26, 2026, federal authorities announced court-authorized domain seizures disrupting two complementary hacking platforms, QScan and QTRouter. Court documents and joint government advisories describe QTFY, a China state-sponsored infrastructure provider associated with Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company, as the operator serving clients that included China’s Ministry of State Security and People’s Liberation Army. Operating since 2018, QScan ran automated reconnaissance with vulnerability scans, while QTRouter obfuscated operational traffic. Intrusions and scanning ranged from unsuccessful access attempts against the U.S. Senate, Department of Health and Human Services, and power utilities to confirmed exploitation against the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, three Department of Energy laboratories, the National Institutes of Health, defense contractors, and financial institutions. Authorities disabled the platforms by seizing the hard-coded control-plane and service domains that made authentication and communication possible.

Closed-Loop Reconnaissance and Automated Exploitation

Explained Viktor Bulanek, founder of AI penetration testing company Penetrify, “A scanner alone produces a list of possibilities, most of which are false or unreachable in practice, and a human then spends the expensive hours deciding which possibilities are real. Wiring the exploit engine to the scanner collapses the loop. The system does not report ‘port open, version vulnerable’; it attempts the exploit, confirms actual access, and then feeds what it just gained back into the next round of scanning from the new vantage point. That feedback loop is the whole point; it converts reconnaissance from a static inventory into a self-extending process where each confirmed foothold rescopes the scan.” Bulanek engineered a similar automated penetration testing pipeline, providing insight into how QTFY weaponized the design for state operations.

Functioning as a distributed task-processing platform, QScan used a RabbitMQ task server to assign jobs to scanner workers and a Redis service to gather results. The system executed webpage scraping, certificate harvesting, subdomain enumeration, and vulnerability verification using a library of more than 200 Python proof-of-concept exploits. Upon identifying responsive edge devices, QScan attempted exploitation without human triage, while separate QTFY botnet-management systems enrolled compromised devices into its proxy network.

“For an IoT-heavy target set that matters even more, because the devices are numerous, homogeneous, and rarely patched, so an automated confirm-and-pivot loop turns a class of weak devices into a reliable entry pipeline without human attention per device,” said Bulanek. “The architecture is not exotic; it is the natural design once you decide a machine, not a person, will do the deciding.”

Obfuscating Attack Streams Across Residential IP Networks

Michael Nizich, assistant dean and director of the Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense Education at New York Institute of Technology, said “The consumer hardware in this case is the routers in our own homes and businesses. It appears to be about making the attack look like it is coming from a constantly changing population of unrelated networks, which may be why they chose this approach. That is why IP reputation alone is a weak control against this architecture.”

QTRouter operated as a layer of a broader obfuscation architecture rather than as a proxy mesh. Running custom OpenWrt firmware at the edge and employing Clash routing software, QTRouter chained connections across commercial proxy services, cloud IPs, and compromised IoT hardware. Multiplexing attack streams across diverse residential networks decouples adversaries from physical egress addresses. When malicious traffic originates from dynamic residential DHCP pools alongside legitimate browsing, static IP scoring models suffer high false-positive rates, limiting efficacy for IP reputation feeds, CIDR blocklists, and geolocation controls, experts said.

The Engineering Economics of Hard-Coded Infrastructure

Damon Rouse, senior lead information security engineer at Black Lotus Labs, a cybersecurity research division of Lumen Technologies, said state-backed developers accept central dependency risks in hard-coded domains in return for operational simplicity, centralized orchestration, and stealth. Fixed service endpoints eliminate the operational complexity of generating domains dynamically, letting operators manage traffic across multi-tenant networks from a single hub while relying on back-end proxy layers for cover.  

Hard-coding control domains can ease deployment but create critical centralized dependencies in the Domain Name System (DNS). QScan and QTRouter implants relied on these fixed domain structures for communications and authentication without secondary fallback channels, so federal domain seizures rendered the known platform implementations inoperable, severing tasking queues, agent authentication, and control channels worldwide. 

Scaling Reach and Velocity Through Outsourced Infrastructure

Moving from custom, in-house military pipelines to a provider of shared infrastructure transforms the operational economics of state-sponsored espionage. According to Rouse, outsourcing infrastructure management to a centralized contractor creates efficiencies across four core dimensions: operational focus; economies of scale; campaign velocity; and attribution cover. By offloading hardware acquisition, scanner development, and proxy management overhead to a third-party contractor like QTFY, state-sponsored operators can concentrate on target exploitation and reaching their objectives. This centralized model democratizes top-tier capabilities and can allow smaller or less-resourced units to rival the reach of an elite cyber program by drawing from shared bandwidth and pre-built tooling.

Outsourcing infrastructure alters offensive software economics. Centralized managed stacks convert fixed development costs into scalable compute overhead, allowing state operators to execute parallel campaigns without dedicating engineering hours to setup.

Rouse said this approach shrinks operational setup. Operators don’t have to pause between campaigns to provision new infrastructure; they just pull pre-configured routing paths and freshly scanned targets directly off the provider’s shelf. Funneling distinct threat groups through identical commercial proxy layers scrambles attribution. It conflates independent espionage units and makes defenders untangle common infrastructure rather than track a single threat actor.

This shared operational model complicates traditional threat intelligence attribution frameworks, as is the case in the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis. When distinct APT groups route payloads through identical QTRouter egress nodes, network-level indicators become shared vendor artifacts, not signatures specifying particular threat groups. Security analysts observing Layer 3 and Layer 4 network telemetry cannot reliably isolate specific threat actors when transport infrastructure reflects the provider’s baseline proxy network rather than a tenant’s unique operational identity.

Unmasking Malicious Flows Within Commercial Proxy Streams

Guofei Gu, Eppright Professor in Engineering and director of the SUCCESS Lab at Texas A&M University, said effective detection in legitimate proxy networks relies on multi-signal behavior correlation across time, network flows, and infrastructure relationships rather than static IP signatures. Advanced detection engines must evaluate temporal telemetry, such as connection sequences, flow duration, port anomalies, and transitions from broad scanning to selective target connections. While individual signals like periodic beaconing or connection failures appear benign alone, correlating the behaviors across hosts exposes the underlying operation, he said.

Effective detection requires DNS relationship mapping and active probing, Gu said. Analyzing co-occurrence patterns among domains, IP addresses, certificates, and client endpoints while interacting with suspicious infrastructure can reveal malicious backends that passive traffic observation cannot detect on its own.

Segmenting Edge Assets to Neutralize Compromised Hardware

Said Tom Hegel, Distinguished Threat Researcher at cybersecurity company SentinelOne, “It comes down to designing the network so that a fully compromised IoT device still has almost nowhere useful to go. This would be something like blocking both its direct access to core assets and indirect access through controllers, recorders, gateways, and management systems,”

“Networks can be configured very tightly so an IoT device can communicate outbound as needed, with strict restrictions on how it communicates,” said Hegel. “Depending on the type of device, that could be something like it only being allowed to communicate outbound over a specific network protocol, to a specific destination, and never being able to reach internal network devices. The specific method used completely depends on how much Internet access the IoT device needs, and how specifically it needs to function inside a network.”

Enforcing egress filtering requires explicit destination IP and FQDN allowlists, combined with strict protocol and transport encryption policies. Blocking arbitrary outbound TCP and UDP connections prevents compromised firmware from establishing reverse shells or connecting with external relay networks, while isolating management planes onto dedicated out-of-band networks keeps edge hardware from reaching gateway controllers.

Fingerprinting Multi-Tenant Espionage Infrastructure

Borja Rodriguez, head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity company Outpost24, said, “[The] reuse [of] the same certificates, registration patterns, and hosting fingerprints across victims with nothing in common [exposes multi-tenant infrastructure]. A single-client pipeline gets built and discarded for one operation, so overlap gives it away.”

In multi-tenant attack infrastructure, vendor shortcuts create shared technical footprints across unrelated campaigns. Unlike single-use pipelines built for one target, shared operational vendors use standardized provisioning scripts and centralized orchestration backends. When incident response teams find recurring artifacts, including reused X.509 TLS certificates, across unrelated sectors, such as energy and higher education, the forensic overlaps distinguish commercial espionage platforms from bespoke pipelines and reveal a centralized infrastructure vendor serving multiple state clients.

David Geer is a journalist who focuses on issues related to cybersecurity. He writes from Cleveland, OH, USA.

item.title: AI Coding Shifts Cognitive Load and Hits Developer Productivity
item.dc:creator: Amy Buttell
item.description: Developers working with agentic AI code must understand code they didn’t write, make sure it works, and see that it fits into the rest of the system.
item.content:encoded:
Traditional measurements of developer productivity—including lines of code written, number of commits, or tickets closed—capture only a small fraction of the work developers perform in the age of AI coding platforms. 

That’s why evaluating developer productivity with traditional tools has the potential to not only increase developer cognitive load, but could also lead to lower developer productivity. Because AI has changed the work developers do, the methods traditionally used to gauge developer productivity create the potential for increased developer mistakes, higher organizational operational failures, slower onboarding and knowledge transfer among teams, and developer burn-out and retention challenges.

“Measuring activity metrics alone pretty much never works,” said Jenna Butler, principal applied research science manager at Microsoft. “Is that really the goal, or is the goal to have good, secure software that meets the needs of the customer? That’s so hard to measure—you need to be a lot more creative.”

At the same time developer cognitive loads are shifting—and, some believe, increasing—the role of software developers is changing, as AI subsumes what used to be the principal job of a developer. The change in the developer job description from writing code to reviewing AI-assisted or generated code contributes to where, when, and how developers experience cognitive load.1

“Every developer who spent his whole life just writing software now has to rebuild himself into a manager,” said Asia Solnyshkina, founder and CEO at ProSense.digital, a consulting firm that builds software and AI products. “It doesn’t matter whether you manage real people or an AI machine, it’s still management. Management itself, taking responsibility for your actions, is exactly what creates the mental overload.”

Today, organizations and teams all too often measure developer productivity based on surface activity metrics. But to improve productivity, reduce cognitive load, avoid risk, and improve the developer experience, experts say organizations and teams can focus on return on investment, adopt emerging productivity metrics, reduce friction before adding more AI into the software development lifecycle, assess the cost versus benefits of AI assisted coding—and more. 

AI Coding Affects Developer Cognitive Load

As AI-assisted coding tools and agentic AI write more code, and developers spend more time reviewing code, developers are grappling with a shifting cognitive load. That’s because they must build understanding of code they didn’t write, check that the code actually does what was intended, and that it fits appropriately into the rest of the system.2

For developers, like everyone else, cognitive load increases as their brains work harder to understand something. Developers experience lower cognitive load when they work in an area where they have significant prior knowledge—like writing code—and increased cognitive load in an area where they lack familiarity.

Reading and reviewing code is a far different task than writing code, and one that imposes a higher cognitive load, said Felienne Hermans, a professor of computer science at Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. “A goal of doing a pull request or analyzing code is to gain an understanding of what is happening with the code,” she said. “You might ask the person who wrote the code, and they tell you the reason. But at least you know what the intent is and even if you have to review fifty pull requests a day, you’ll have some fatigue.”

“This checking fatigue is also true for AI-generated code,” she said. “If developers are looking at AI-generated code, it seems to be fine, even if it isn’t. The result is that bad code will go in, and developers at the same time are not building mental models of what the code is designed to accomplish, which creates less and less understanding in the code base as time goes on.”

The Developer Productivity Challenge

Even before AI-assisted coding tools became more common, developer productivity did not lend itself particularly well to measurement. That’s because the factors involved in measuring developer productivity are complex.

“Developer productivity is a confounding factor because it is very hard to measure,” said Hermans. “Because managers don’t understand programming very well, they’ve tried to encapsulate it into something that is measurable, which takes the form of measuring lines of code and story points.” Story points estimate the effort involved to complete a developer task.3

Over time, the industry has developed frameworks designed to measure developer productivity, including:

  • DORA: DevOps Research and Assessment, developed 2014-2018;
  • SPACE: Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication/Collaboration, and Efficiency and flow, developed in 2021; and
  • DevEx: Developer Experience, developed in 2023.

The three productivity frameworks have built upon each other over time and are used in different ways across industry to measure productivity.4 DORA, which is the most widely utilized, is employed as an automated dashboard to track how fast teams ship code.5 SPACE is used as a broad diagnostic checklist to ensure teams are committed to a broad measurement of productivity.6 DevEx is used as a recurring developer survey and systems metric to pinpoint friction in a system.7

Little industry consensus exists on how to measure developer productivity; developers also lack confidence that the measurements organizations use adequately reflect the contributions they make to their organizations.8,9

As AI coding tools and agentic AI coding tools continue to evolve, the role of developers continues to shift towards managing code rather than writing it, which highlights one aspect of software development that is correlated with productivity: developer satisfaction.10

“From the developer experience perspective, one of the central aspects of whether things are going well is how motivated they are, and part of that motivation is that they have some kind of personal and professional pride in their work,” said Fabian Fagerholm, associate professor of computer science at Finland’s Aalto University. “Am I actually producing something of value? Am I the one producing the value, or am I just watching something else produce some value, and I’m supposed to be some kind of gatekeeper?”

How to Measure Developer Productivity Appropriately

While some aspects of measuring developer productivity in relation to AI-assisted coding have changed, others have not, said Butler, one of the authors of the original SPACE productivity framework paper. “A lot hasn’t changed and if anything, people are doubling down on what has never worked, not by lines of code or numbers of pull requests,” she said. “Suddenly, developer productivity matters a lot because there’s a lot of money on the line.”

For Matthew Skelton, co-author of Team Topologies: Organizing Business and Technology for Fast Flow of Value, measuring developer productivity boils down to building a system that is an effective and efficient steward of value and the flow of value across an organization.

“What technologies are appropriate to use?” he asked. “What are the criteria that is needed? Thinking about cognitive load, how can extraneous cognitive load be reduced within the flow of value? Those questions guide us towards using certain technologies in a certain way, because it is very much focused on the ongoing health of that value flow.”

This kind of evaluation holds true when it comes to adding AI tools to an organization. To effectively use such tools to enhance organizational value, organizations must create clearly defined boundaries of responsibility around AI use and assign accountability for outcomes related to focused areas of AI activity, Skelton said.

In regard to more specific measurements of developer productivity, Butler noted the SPACE framework recommends examining several different categories of data to get a handle on developer productivity.11 “Are my developers feeling like they are learning? Are they able to communicate well? What is the quality of the code?” Butler asked. “When developers are happy, they are usually churning out lots of good code.”

“You pick and choose a few metrics from totally different categories that hold each other somewhat in tension, and I think this is still the best way to measure productivity,” she added. “You become agnostic about the AI tool they are using and look at whether the organization is shipping more secure code, whether the number of incidents are down, what the code survivability is, and whether there are more bugs.”

Nethanel Bar, co-founder and CEO at Coddy, a platform that teaches coding, noted that any assessment of developer productivity must be made in the context of how developers impact business development. “Phased roll-out of AI often proves more effective than full-fledged adoption right away, since it allows the team to discover the most beneficial ways to use the technology,” he said. “Adopting new tools gradually, not all at once, is the best way to figure out what works and what does not.”

For Fagerholm, the costs of using large language models (LLMs) are an appropriate question to consider in relation to developer productivity. “We aren’t completely certain how we should measure the cost of a developer using a LLM,” he said. “How can we compare productivity of a developer and an LLM if we think of productivity as the relationship between some kind of input or effort and the output that I get?”

“Developers have a certain salary so we know roughly what they cost, but with an LLM, it has turned out to be very difficult to control costs because developers can rack up large bills trying out different things,” Fagerholm said. “The situation creates a challenge for companies trying to measure the productivity of LLM-assisted development, which are going to need to calculate to determine if it is worth using certain models for certain tasks.”

References

1. Developers’ Experience with Generative AI – First Insights from Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study, ICSE-SEIP ’26: Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice, Pages 259-268 (July 11, 2026); https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3786583.3786870

2. Beyond the Hype: A Comprehensive Review of Current Trends in Generative AI Research, Teaching Practices, and Tools. TiCSE 2024: 2024 Working Group Reports on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education. Association for Computing Machinery (Jan. 23, 2025); https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3689187.3709614

3. Agile Estimating and Planning, Mountain Goat Software; https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/books/agile-estimating-and-planning

4. Agile Alliance, Demystifying Story Points (July 14, 2017); https://agilealliance.org/resources/experience-reports/improving-estimation-story-points/

5. Gitmore.io, What are DORA Metrics? A Practical Guide for Engineering Teams (July 20, 2026); https://gitmore.io/blog/dora-metrics-guide

6. SPACE Framework, The SPACE Framework: A Complete Guide to Developer Productivity (Jan. 4, 2025); https://space-framework.com

7. DevEx: What Actually Drives Productivity, Communications (Nov. 1, 2023); https://cacm.acm.org/practice/devex-what-actually-drives-productivity/

8. SPACEX: Exploring Metrics with the SPACE Model for Developer Productivity (article pre-print), Association for Computing Machinery (Nov. 26, 2025); https://arxiv.org/html/2511.20955v1

9. JetBrains, The State of Developer Experience and Developer Productivity: What Developers Truly Want (Oct. 15, 2025); https://devecosystem-2025.jetbrains.com/productivity

10. Towards a Theory of Software Developer Job Satisfaction and Perceived Productivity, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (September 2019); https://bit.ly/3X7H60d

11. The SPACE of Developer Productivity, Communications (June 1, 2021); https://cacm.acm.org/practice/the-space-of-developer-productivity/

Amy Buttell is a Silver Spring, MD-based technology, legal, and business journalist, content creator, writer, and ghostwriter.

item.title: Sharing AI’s Gains
item.dc:creator: James Larus
item.description: A company that replaces an employee with AI should be required to share some of the resulting savings with that employee.
item.content:encoded:
As Editor-in-Chief of Communications, I dream of the day I can replace my editorial board and reviewers with AI. No more editorial turnover and constant recruiting, no more waiting weeks or months for a review, no more one-line reviews or ambiguous recommendations, and no more management of 100+ volunteers. Just click a button, and a few minutes later, three assured, well-written evaluations of a submission and a recommendation appear. I’m confident that most journal editors and program committee chairs share my fantasy.

My fantasy is harmless because I do not intend to act on it. If you read my earlier editorial about Communications and AI,a you might suspect I do not plan to replace my editorial board with AI. As facile, quick, and capable as AI appears, it lacks the perspective and judgment essential to review and edit material written by people for human readers. In industry, however, the same economic temptation is increasingly real—and the people making the decision do not bear most of its human cost.

We’ve all seen CEOs and CFOs who not only share this vision but put it into effect by laying off employees and replacing them with AI. Their company’s stock price soars, their stock options become more valuable, and why not? They’re riding the wave of the future while cutting operating costs. The financial gains accrue to the company and its shareholders, while much of the cost—lost income, disrupted careers, and damaged communities—is borne by workers and society. Perhaps concerns will change when AI starts replacing CEOs and CFOs, but right now the C-suite doesn’t seem too worried about AI’s effect on their (former) employees.

At the same time, you might not feel comfortable with the CEOs’ motivations. The rise of private equity in America and the “enshittification”b of many products and services demonstrates that many industrial leaders prioritize returns to investors over quality, and that finding new ways to cut costs takes priority over long-term reputations.

I have a modest proposal to push back against this pressure. My proposal is that a company that replaces an employee with AI should be required to share some of the resulting savings with that employee. In economic terms, the company should bear part of the transition cost its decision creates rather than shifting the entire burden onto the worker and society. By law, employers should guarantee every employee half their salary for five years if AI replaces them. It would probably make sense to front-load the payout (e.g., 90%, 70%, 50%, 30%, 10% per year) to cushion the transition and provide incentives and financial support to find a new career. Of course, the obligation would need to be secured, so ex-employees would be first in line if the company declares bankruptcy.

Defining replacement would not be simple. The obligation might be triggered when a company eliminates a position or materially reduces employment in a job category while deploying AI to perform substantially the same work. Rules would also have to prevent evasion through outsourcing, contracting, or attrition.

If AI only offers a small improvement in cost and productivity over an employee, this proposal will make it financially unattractive to disrupt someone’s life. If AI is far cheaper and more productive, the fired worker would share its financial benefits for a fixed period to help them start a new career. The company’s “investment” in AI would not be fully realized for several years. The transition payment would become part of the cost of adopting AI, just like equipment purchase, integration, training, and maintenance costs are today.

From society’s perspective, this would fund support and retraining for people in roles that machines could handle better or cheaper. The funding would come directly from industries that benefit from AI and go directly to people adversely affected by AI. Globalization has shown that economic transformation can benefit society overall while devastating workers and communities. Promises that those workers will be retrained for better jobs have too often proved inadequate. This proposal does not rely on an organized retraining program; instead, it would offer a financial cushion and incentive to find a new career.

This policy would undoubtedly slow some AI adoption. That is a feature, not a flaw, when the financial advantage is too small to compensate for the disruption it causes. Truly transformative uses of AI would still proceed, but workers would share temporarily in the gains they helped make possible. Still, I suspect most people would be happy to see AI adoption proceed more slowly and thoughtfully, with fewer casualties on the road to the future.

item.title: What Happened in Fall 2026: AI and P vs NP
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Viola
item.description: The OpenAI results gave faster algorithms for a number of problems that were conjectured to not admit such improvements.
item.content:encoded:
Theoreticians will never forget 2026. When I left Massachusetts in the summer for a coast-to-coast trip, research in my field, theoretical computer science, was still done the way math had been done for the previous several millennia. Sure, artificial intelligence seemed to be getting better, but hadn’t we been there before? It was natural to be a little skeptical.

But when I arrived in California to attend a program on pseudorandomness1 at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing, I found the field transformed almost beyond recognition. Suddenly, every proof was AI-assisted, and all the talk was about swarms of AI agents and Lean autoformalization. Then, on September 8, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem.2 Still, the impact on theoretical computer science was hard to judge; this was a problem in fluid dynamics, not computer science. Maybe there was something about this problem that made it particularly easy for AI, plus apparently researchers working on the problem who had been using AI models for a while got very close. Maybe OpenAI had somehow used their ideas and just wrapped up the solution faster than them. But soon afterward, rumors started circulating that a merry gang at OpenAI was systematically attacking all major open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, and unbelievably solving a large fraction of them. One of these was a problem central to the program at the Simons Institute: BPL versus L, asking whether randomized algorithms using logarithmic memory can be “derandomized,” that is, simulated deterministically while still using logarithmic memory. Worse, these incredible AI feats were beyond the grasp of publicly available models; only the companies’ internal models were strong enough.

The atmosphere at the Institute became increasingly gloomy. People felt discouraged, hopeless; there didn’t seem to be any point in talking research anymore. I had looked forward to research collaborations with longtime colleagues; instead, we ended up sitting in adjacent rooms, each of us prompting an AI model.

In the evening, I would come back to my rental in the El Cerrito hills to watch the sun set over the bay and San Francisco, where OpenAI’s headquarters are located, pondering the end of the field to which I had devoted 30 years.

Then, another rumor started circulating: OpenAI was going to release its findings on October 6. When that date approached, there was a flood of papers on the Web, as researchers rushed to post whatever partial results they had in order to secure some recognition before the OpenAI release.

When October 6 finally came and OpenAI indeed released its findings,3 there was a party at the Institute. Finally, the tension was released, and there was something to look at. But the atmosphere soon became somber again. The OpenAI dump contained solutions to hundreds of major mathematical problems, many of which had stood for decades and some for over a century. The proofs seemed to originate from an alien mind. They were the product of gigantic datacenters, scattered over desolate parts of the globe and effectively turning Mother Earth into a motherboard.

The results in theoretical computer science were absolutely eye-popping. They were like looking into the next 20 years of theoretical breakthroughs, condensed into a single moment. Matrix multiplication, BPL, unique games, fast Fourier transform, and countless more; each would require a separate post to convey the magnitude of the improvement.

Yet there was something that shocked many people even more. Many of the results countered long-held conjectures related to the grand challenge of theoretical computer science, and my main area of research: understanding the power and limitations of efficient computation. The most famous instance is the P versus NP problem,4 another Millennium Prize Problem, but one that has not yet been solved. In a nutshell, it asks whether a prominent class of problems—including the satisfiability of Boolean formulae and the traveling salesman problem—admits efficient algorithms, running in time nc for a constant c on inputs of length n. Virtually all researchers believe these problems cannot be solved efficiently, and thus that P is not equal to NP.

The AI results did not prove that P equals NP, but they did give several faster algorithms for a number of problems that were conjectured to not admit such improvements.

First, on October 5, Alman and Vassilevska Williams released a paper5 explaining an algorithm discovered by an internal model at Anthropic that disproves the 3SUM conjecture. Stated in the 1990s,6 this conjecture asserts that deciding if three numbers sum to zero in a given list of n numbers requires time quadratic in n, a time which can be essentially achieved by an undergraduate-level algorithm using sorting and binary search. Anthropic’s new algorithm solves the problem in less time. This development is especially significant because in the last three decades, researchers had been using the 3SUM conjecture as a basis to settle the complexity of many other problems. The falsity of the 3SUM conjecture means that all these problems must now be re-examined.

Second, as part of the October 6 dump, OpenAI presented an algorithm to multiply two n-bit integers faster than n log n,7 something conjectured to be impossible in the 1970s.8

And finally, the biggest blow of all: on October 26, OpenAI proved that the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false.9 Introduced in the late 1990s,10 this conjecture is a strengthening of the conjecture that P is different from NP. It states that Boolean satisfiability not only cannot be solved in time nc for a constant c, but in fact requires exponential time, even for restricted formulae in conjunctive normal form with three literals per clause. Like the 3SUM conjecture, but to a much greater extent, this hypothesis underpinned decades of research. While the most glaring consequence of OpenAI’s discovery is to remove the basis for many subsequent works, the discovery has other consequences as well. For example, it yields a circuit-size lower bound of the order for a “half-explicit” function on n bits computable in exponential time,11 while we still do not know if explicit functions such as Boolean satisfiability admit circuits of size 10 n.

These and other new findings actually support my iconoclastic belief that P equals NP. I have articulated the reasons behind my belief in my book Mathematics of the Impossible12 and in my 2018 blog post, “I believe P=NP.”13 Part of the “evidence” I collected is a comprehensive list of historical examples showing that researchers have consistently underestimated the power of efficient computation. Therefore, if one is to extrapolate from history, I believe the only reasonable direction is toward P equals NP. I expect that even more conjectures will fall soon.

The future of the field lies with AI. The community must get together and build smarter and faster AI tools, trained by and publicly accessible to all researchers. With them, we will finally settle P vs NP.

References

1. Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. Pseudorandomness & High-Dimensional Expansion (2026).

2. OpenAI. On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem (Sept. 8, 2026).

3. OpenAI. Sharing AI progress in mathematics (Oct. 6, 2026).

4. Clay Mathematics Institute. P vs NP.

5. Alman, J. and Vassilevska Williams, V. Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs. arXiv:2610.06783 (Oct. 5, 2026).

6. Gajentaan, A. and Overmars, M.H. On a class of O(n²) problems in computational geometry. Computational Geometry 5, 3 (1995), 165–185.

7. OpenAI. Integer multiplication below n log n. Manuscript dated Sept. 23, 2026; released Oct. 6, 2026.

8. Schönhage, A. and Strassen, V. Schnelle Multiplikation großer Zahlen. Computing 7 (1971), 281–292.

9. OpenAI. The Exponential Time Hypothesis Is False (Oct. 25, 2026).

10. Impagliazzo, R. and Paturi, R. Complexity of k-SAT. Proceedings of the 14th Annual IEEE Conference on Computational Complexity (1999), 237–240.

11. Jahanjou, H., Miles, E., and Viola, E. Local reduction. Information and Computation 261, Part 2 (2018), 281–295.

12. Viola, E. Mathematics of the Impossible: The Complexity of Computation. Cambridge University Press (Expected publication July 2027).

13. Viola, E. I believe P=NP. Thoughts (Feb. 16, 2018).

14. Viola, E. Thoughts (2026).

Emanuele Viola is a professor of computer science at Northeastern University, the author of numerous research papers and the forthcoming Cambridge University Press book Mathematics of the Impossible, and a former video game developer. His honors include an NSF CAREER Award, a Computational Complexity Conference Best Paper Award, and a SIAM Student Paper Prize; he blogs at Thoughts.14

item.title: Can We Understand the Inner Workings of LLMs?
item.dc:creator: Bennie Mols
item.description: Researchers are using tools from causality theory to understand the keys to an algorithm working at a higher level of abstraction.
item.content:encoded:
Large language models (LLMs) can write essays, solve math problems, and generate computer code. But nobody fully understands how they do it. Researchers can observe billions of parameters inside these systems changing during training, yet the internal logic of the models remains largely hidden. In a sense, the engineering is ahead of the science. Can science catch up and make LLMs and other deep neural networks mechanistically interpretable?

One of the researchers in this growing field is Thomas Icard, professor of philosophy and computer science at Stanford University. Icard is contributing to this effort using tools from logic and cognitive science. “It’s striking how much progress there already has been in the last few years on basically every dimension,” Icard said. “From how much a model’s behaviors and representations reflect patterns in training data, and how post-training reshapes that behavior, to deep connections between internalized abstractions and generalization.”

A central question in this field is whether neural networks merely mimic reasoning, or do they internally build elements of a logical or algorithmic reasoning system. One approach to investigating this question is a framework known as causal abstraction,a developed by Icard together with his students and collaborators. It provides a rigorous way of asking whether computations inside a neural network correspond to an interpretable algorithm at a higher level of abstraction.

“Of course, a neural network implements algorithms at a very low level of abstraction,” Icard said, “involving matrix multiplications and the like. But we are searching for concepts that are more intuitive and interpretable, such as those explored in cognitive science, linguistics, and logic.”

This search resembles the way physicists abstract from the statistical behavior of individual molecules to the ideal gas law, which describes a gas in terms of pressure and temperature rather than in terms of colliding particles. In the simplest analogy for neural networks, the activity of many individual neurons can similarly be grouped into the behavior of a single higher-level computational unit. Yet real neural networks can exhibit much more complicated forms of abstraction, because individual neurons can contribute simultaneously to many different functions.

The central question, then, is when two descriptions at different levels of abstraction can nevertheless refer to the same underlying process. Icard: “If you have two causal models that are formulated in different languages with different variables, when do you want to say that one is a more abstract description of the same underlying causal reality as the other? This is called causal abstraction and we build on existing theory, adapting it to the study of neural networks in particular.”

In a 2001 study,b Icard and his collaborators – led by then-Ph.D. student, now leading researcher in the field Atticus Geigerc – showed that a BERT-based language model internally implements elements of a logical reasoning system. For example, the model learned an internal algorithm for performing complex logical inferences involving quantifiers (“every,” “some,” “not,” etc.) and negation.

Since that early work, other researchers have also begun uncovering examples of the algorithms that language models develop internally. An example that recently generated a lot of attention comes from the paper Arithmetic in the Wild: Llama uses Base-10 Addition to Reason About Cyclic Conceptsd by researchers at Goodfire AI, led again by Geiger. The researchers studied how a Llama-based language model reasons over cyclic concepts, for example: “What month is six months after August?” One might expect the model to calculate directly within a 12-month cycle. Instead, the model first uses standard decimal addition: August is treated internally as month 8, after which the model calculates 6 + 8 = 14. Only then does it translate the result 14 back to “February,” as 14 = 12 + 2, and February is the second month.

The Llama-based model uses this method not only to reason about months, but also about weekdays and clock time. The model thus applies the same general calculation strategy to different types of problems, without explicitly being instructed to do so. Said Icard, “The paper is a beautiful example of using causal abstraction methods to uncover how a large language model reasons about cyclic concepts.”

Another studye from 2026 by Nikhil Prakash and colleagues examines a very different type of reasoning: keeping track of what different characters know. Researchers gave language models simple stories in which two people interact with different objects and may or may not be able to observe each other. For example, Bob fills a bottle with beer and Carla fills a cup with coffee, while Bob can observe Carla’s actions. Later the model is asked: “What does Bob believe the cup contains?” To answer correctly, the model has to connect several pieces of information: Bob is the person whose belief matters; the cup is the object being asked about; coffee is the cup’s contents; and Bob saw Carla fill it, so Bob knows this.

The researchers found evidence that the model does this in several stages. It starts by internally linking together the relevant character, object, and state; for instance, Bob, cup, and coffee. When the question arrives, it uses the words in the question as a kind of pointer to “look back” to the earlier part of the story and retrieve the relevant information.

Yet another 2026 studyf by Yoav Gur-Arieh and colleagues shows that language models can combine several internal strategies to keep track of relationships between entities. Suppose the model reads the sentences “Pete loves jam, Ann loves pie, Tim loves tea” and is then asked: “Who loves pie?” It has to remember that ‘Ann’ is associated with ‘pie’. The researchers found that models use several strategies at once to retrieve the right association. One is to remember where the pair ‘Ann – pie’ occurred in the list. Another is to use the word ‘pie’ itself to retrieve the name associated with it. A third uses an internal pointer that leads directly back to ‘Ann.’

In short lists, remembering position often works well. In longer lists, especially for items in the middle, this strategy becomes less reliable, and the other two strategies work better. The researchers found the same basic pattern across nine LLMs.

Taken together, these studies show that researchers are beginning to uncover some of the internal strategies LLMs use to reason. Turning such individual findings into a broader understanding of these systems, however, remains a major challenge.

One practical limitation is access to the models themselves. Academic researchers can only do their experiments on open-source LLMs like Llama by Meta and OLMo by the Allen Institute for AI. “The largest models we have worked with contain around a trillion parameters,” Icard said. “In our experiments, we go inside and change the weights or the activations in the neural network. We do not have access to the commercial models, but I do know that some companies, such as Anthropic and Google DeepMind, do have teams working on mechanistic interpretability of large language models. We regularly talk with both these groups.”

Researchers are now exploring whether mechanistic interpretability can help make LLMs safer, more reliable, and more efficient, while also reducing unwanted biases. “I think there is promise for all of those,” said Icard. Major challenges remain, however, such as scaling these techniques to larger models and automating parts of the interpretability process that currently still depend heavily on human insight.

“Mechanistic interpretability will probably never reduce large language models to a few simple equations,” Icard concludes, “but it may gradually turn deep neural networks into systems whose hidden algorithms can at least partly be understood.” If so, the science of LLMs may finally be catching up with the engineering.

item.title: In Memoriam: Margaret Hamilton (1936-2026)
item.dc:creator: John Delaney
item.description: Hamilton was renowned for designing software that anticipated and fixed failures before they happened, which helped define what reliable software engineering looks like today.
item.content:encoded:
Margaret Hamilton, who led the team that created the on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo command and lunar modules that took men to the Moon in 1969, has died at the age of 90.

Hamilton was renowned for designing software that anticipated failures before they happened, as well as helping to define what reliable software engineering looks like today.

She was the recipient of numerous accolades and honors, which recognized her legacy that reshaped both spaceflight and modern software engineering. Hamilton was an ACM Distinguished Member and in 2003, NASA presented her with its Exceptional Space Act Award. In 2016, Hamilton received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor in the U.S., for her contributionsa “to concepts of asynchronous software, priority scheduling and priority displays, and human-in-the-loop decision capability, which set the foundation for modern, ultra-reliable software design and engineering.”

Margaret Heafield was born on August 17, 1936, in Paoli, IN, the oldest of four children. She began studying mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955, then transferred to Earlham College in Richmond, IN, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics in 1958. That same year, she married James Hamilton, and the couple moved to Cambridge, Massachusetts, the following year while he attended Harvard Law School.

In 1959, Hamilton started her career at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in MIT’s meteorology department, which introduced her to computer programming. In 1961, Hamilton moved to MIT’s Lincoln Laboratory, where she worked on SAGE,b an early U.S. Air Force air-defense system that used computers to identify potentially hostile aircraft. This work sparked her interest in software reliability, which was a newly emerging field at the time.

In 1965, Hamilton joined MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory after it won a NASA contract to develop the onboard guidance software for the Apollo missions. She was the first programmer hired for the Apollo project, as well as its first female programmer.

Initially assigned to uncrewed missions, Hamilton advanced to lead the team responsible for the onboard flight software used in crewed Apollo flights. By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. Ultimately, she led about 100 engineers, while more than 400 people contributed to Apollo software overall.

Hamilton prioritized defensive programming, which grew in part from an incident involving Lauren, her daughter. In a commemorationc of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing, Hamilton recounted how while playing with an Apollo command-module simulator, Lauren initiated a pre-launch program during simulated flight and crashed the system. Hamilton proposed a software safeguard, but the idea was initially rejected because it was presumed the astronauts were unlikely to make that error. During the Apollo 8 flight in 1968, astronaut Jim Lovell inadvertently triggered the same command Lauren had, causing navigational data to disappear. Hamilton and her team resolved the problem, and her proposed protections were subsequently incorporated into the system.

The most decisive demonstration of Hamilton’s work came during Apollo 11’s lunar landing on July 20, 1969. Minutes before the Eagle lunar module was supposed to touch down on the moon, its computer generated an alarm because it was overloaded by unnecessary tasks. Hamilton’s priority-driven software recognized the overload and discarded lower-priority work while preserving the functions needed for landing. Mission Control trusted the system and continued the descent, which enabled Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the moon. In time, Hamilton would work on the subsequent lunar landings, Skylab, and early planning for space shuttle missions.

Perhaps Hamilton’s most enduring achievement was helping to establish software engineering as a serious engineering discipline. She popularized the term “software engineering” and conveyed that software development required the same rigor, testing, and accountability as hardware engineering. Hamilton’s team developed techniques that anticipated errors, prioritized critical tasks, and allowed systems to recover safely from unexpected conditions. As Apollo’s onboard computers had extremely limited processing power and memory, these methods were essential.

“I fought to legitimize software so that both this engineering discipline and the people who built it would receive the respect they deserved. That is why I began using the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other forms of engineering,” Hamilton recalled in a 2014 interviewd with El Pais. “When I started using those words, people found them funny. Software eventually earned the same respect as any other discipline.”

After its work on the Apollo program ended in the mid-1970s, the MIT Instrumentation Lab was spun off by MIT and evolved into Draper Laboratory.

“Margaret left an indelible mark on Draper, and we will be forever grateful,” said Jerry M. Wohletz, president and CEO at Draper. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.”

Hamilton declined to join Draper after it was spun off from MIT and became a software entrepreneur instead. In 1976, she founded Higher Order Software, which applied her principles of fault tolerance and error prevention. She later founded Hamilton Technologies, which developed the Universal Systems Language for designing reliable complex systems.

On the 40th anniversary of the moon landing in 2009, Hamilton distillede her experience with the Apollo program: “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust. We had to find a way and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”

Margaret Hamilton is survived by her daughter Lauren Hamilton and son-in-law Richard Selesnick, as well as two grandsons and four great-grandchildren. She is also survived by her siblings, John, David, and Kathryn Heafield.

item.title: When a Model Writes Uzbek in Three Alphabets
item.dc:creator: Ivan Lapa
item.description: How to get a model to understand Uzbek written in Cyrillic, in classical Latin, and in Latin with apostrophes.
item.content:encoded:
When a team in Tashkent or Almaty ships an AI feature, whether a support bot, menu search, or voice-note parsing, the first debate is almost always about the model: which one understands Uzbek, whether to use a Kazakhstan-built model, whether GPT is good enough. Most failures happen upstream of the model. One user writes Uzbek in Cyrillic, another in Latin, a third in Latin with three different apostrophes, and many messages are partly Russian. A model that looks strong on a benchmark behaves very differently on that stream.

The script problem is about to get harder. Uzbekistan began moving from Cyrillic to Latin script in 1993; the deadline for the change slipped from 2000 to 2005, 2010, and then 2023, and both scripts remain in wide use. On October 21, 2026, Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev signed a law revising the Latin alphabet itself: from April 22, 2027, sh becomes Ş, ch becomes Ç, o‘ becomes Ö, and g‘ becomes Ğ, with no single deadline for the switch. Uzbek text will arrive in three written forms, because old text and typing habits remain. Even today, o‘ is typed as oʻ, o’, o` or o’, since the correct character isn’t on a standard keyboard. A person reads one word; your search index, tokenizer, and string matching see four. Kazakhstan’s own Latin transition still has no timeline, and Kazakh online is mostly Cyrillic, with Russian mixed in mid-sentence.

What do the benchmarks say? KazMMLU, comprised of about 23,000 questions in Kazakh and Russian, offers two lessons. Global frontier models lead by a wide margin: with Kazakh instructions, GPT-4o averages 76.7% accuracy, while two Kazakh-specialized eight-billion-parameter models land around 38–39%. And results depend on the language of the instructions in ways that vary by model: GPT-4o barely moves between English and Kazakh instructions, while in the KazMMLU paper’s tables DeepSeek V3 falls from 76.9% to 45.5%. That is one model in one run, but the practical lesson holds: test with the exact prompt you will ship.

TUMLU is unusual in testing both scripts. On Kazakh, all three tested models performed better in the Cyrillic script, and Latin-script prompts often pushed them into output that resembled Tatar. On Uzbek, the script made little difference (Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored 67.9 in Cyrillic, and 68.6 in Latin), because Uzbek text online is split more evenly. The paper also carries a warning: Uzbek looked most difficult partly because its questions were modeled on university entrance exams. Comparing languages by one number from someone else’s benchmark mostly compares the people who wrote the questions.

Three more gaps matter for products. Code-switching is barely studied: researchers working on Kazakh-Russian translation found no public parallel corpus and built one of 618 sentences. For voice, the Whisper paper found that recognition error roughly halves with every sixteen-fold increase in training data for a language, so strong Russian recognition says nothing about Uzbek. And tokenizers can turn the same text into sequences up to fifteen times longer depending on the language, which moves price, latency, and how much history fits in context. Count tokens per message for each language and script in your own traffic before you sign off on unit economics.

So normalize before the model. Detect language and script per message, not per user profile: the same person may type Latin on a phone in the morning and Cyrillic on a laptop at night. Map all apostrophe variants to one canonical character in a copy used for search and matching, and keep the original. Index both scripts, using transliteration tables built with a native speaker and tested on real dish, street, and product names. Don’t convert Kazakh to Latin before the model for consistency’s sake, since TUMLU suggests Cyrillic works better. Reply in the script the user wrote in. And store the alphabet version as a data field, so that a search conducted after April 2027 finds a word in any spelling without relabeling the archive.

Then build your own evaluation set from real requests, split into strata: Uzbek Cyrillic, Uzbek Latin (soon in both orthographies), Kazakh, Russian, mixed messages, and voice. Score each stratum separately; if most traffic is Russian, an overall average will hide a failure on Uzbek Cyrillic. Use native-speaker labelers from different generations, since people schooled before and after the switch to Latin write differently, and trust an LLM judge only on strata where you have checked it against human ratings.

Finally, treat fallback as a product decision. Some users will accept a Russian reply to an Uzbek question; others will read it as a sign that the product wasn’t built for them. When confidence is low, ask a clarifying question in the user’s language or offer buttons. In payments, safety, or account blocks, route to a person who speaks the language. Offer Russian as a choice rather than switching silently, and log every fallback with its language and script, because a month of logs shows where the model fails systematically.

Where to start? Pull a week of real messages and label them by language and script. It takes a couple of days and shows what traffic you are actually serving. You can swap a model in a week; your normalization layer and evaluation set will outlast several model changes and the move to Uzbekistan’s new Latin alphabet.

Disclosure: The views expressed are my own and do not necessarily reflect those of my employer.

Ivan Lapa is a product manager at Uzum Tezkor in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. He previously worked on courier products at Yandex Pro.

item.title: AI’s Accuracy Nears the Best Human Forecasters
item.dc:creator: Samuel Greengard
item.description: AI models' forecasting accuracy has climbed steadily and is nearing parity with the best human forecasters.
item.content:encoded:
When business leaders, government officials, and others seek predictability in a highly unpredictable world, they turn to forecasts. Historically, the most accurate prognostications have come from a group of humans called superforecasters, who weigh probabilities and analyze questions before reaching conclusions.

These individuals—the top 2% of forecasters—perform about 30% better than professional intelligence analysts with access to classified information, according to research conducted by Barbara Mellers and Philip Tetlock. But now things are getting more complicated as AI forecasting enters the picture.

“AI has transformed trading in prediction markets and in financial markets more generally,” said Rajiv Sethi, a professor of economics at Barnard College, Columbia University, and an external professor at the Santa Fe Institute. “Now there’s a question of whether superforecasters will become obsolete due to the AI revolution.”

According to ForecastBench, a benchmarking tool that scores AI models against human forecasters, model accuracy has climbed steadily over the past two years, reaching near parity with superforecasters. Yet parity isn’t judgment, and a growing number of observers are concerned that profit incentives and a lack of visibility into how prediction systems function could invite trouble.

A growing question is whether it’s acceptable to trade explanation for accuracy. “We’re not yet at a point where anyone is willing to take the best forecasting models and rely on them for high-stakes decisions,” said Ezra Karger, a senior economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago who leads the team that built ForecastBench.

Guessing Games

It is not surprising that forecasters would turn to AI to unravel complex geopolitical and economic events. LLMs can digest thousands of pages of reports in seconds and spot connections that humans miss. They excel at predicting the next word—though that’s far from predicting the outcome of world events.

Already, a handful of startups are looking to reinvent the way forecasting takes place. While the approaches of these firms, including FutureSearch, Mantic, and Sooth Labs vary, all rely on a frontier language model and software that decomposes questions, directs searches, weighs conflicting information, and returns a calibrated probability with a written rationale.

For example, U.K.-based Mantic describes its mission as predicting “like an expert human forecaster but with digital speed and scale.” The firm focuses on geopolitics, business, policy, and technology anywhere from one week to one year out. Sooth Labs claims that it “delivers reliable forecasts to the questions that matter most,” helping “allocate capital, manage risk, and act with insight, not instinct.”

Those claims have faced at least one public test. In the Metaculus Cup, Mantic’s system finished fourth against 539 human forecasters. Entrants had predicted the top bot would score 40% compared to human predictions, yet Mantic topped 80%.

Tests like this are possible because predictions eventually play out in the real world, and scoring across many forecasts separates skill from luck. “One critical factor is gathering important context, and the other is reasoning about the context, weighing this evidence, and coming up with a forecast,” said Shashwat Goel, a former research intern at Meta and currently a Ph.D. student at the ELLIS Institute in Tübingen, Germany.

Goel, who studies ways to train and evaluate AI forecasters, pointed out that there’s little uniformity in the prediction space. Forecast methods can vary greatly across questions and across human and machine systems. A U.S. general election or interest rate hike produces mountains of data, while a conflict in sub-Saharan Africa or software release date may hinge on an obscure document.

AI’s real edge is sheer scale. Many human superforecasters are hobbyists who enjoy the process but face time limitations, Goel said. Models can search relentlessly, yet there’s a catch: faster retrieval doesn’t mean better judgment. “Right now, most performance is driven by the quality of web search,” he explained.

Blind Spots

Gauging the accuracy of AI prediction systems remains tricky. “Success” depends on the criteria a scoring system applies—typically a Brier score, which measures how far a forecaster’s assigned probability landed from the outcome. Yet, scoreboards look backward, so it can take months or even years to learn whether a prediction was correct.

Backtests speed the process. They work because a model’s training ends at a fixed cutoff date. Events after that date remain unknown to the model, even though they have already taken place. So, while developers can score a model based on settled questions, they may inadvertently feed it information that wasn’t known on the date of the forecast. “It’s very easy for information to leak into a system beyond the cutoff date, and that can reveal the answer,” Goel said.

Guarding against this problem is a significant challenge. It’s difficult to build a closed model or rebuild the information environment as a frozen snapshot. Backtests, no matter how elaborate, can miss this data leakage and produce skewed results. In addition, system builders don’t always adhere to best practices—and sometimes their evaluation methods are “sloppy,” said Daniel Paleka, a Ph.D. student who has studied AI forecasting at ETH Zurich’s SPY Lab.

Paleka is not skeptical of AI’s forecasting ability—he believes it can complement human forecasters through smart data aggregation—but he’s concerned benchmark scores can be wildly inaccurate without a frozen snapshot of the Internet. His testing has revealed that AI forecasting is “broadly reasonable but not ingenious.” Systems roughly match smart humans over the short term, but long-term accuracy remains an open question.

There’s another issue: recruiting superforecasters is slow and costly. As a result, ForecastBench frequently measures today’s models against scores that humans posted roughly two years ago and then applies statistical adjustments. So, what appears to be a dead heat may fall within a margin of error. The takeaway? It is essential not to “overstate” results, Karger said.

Making Prophets

AI in prediction markets introduces a different problem. Venues like Kalshi and Polymarket now accommodate AI agents on their trading platforms. Yet accuracy and profitability are distinct things, Sethi said. An agent might make money by baiting rival bots into desirable responses, then trading against them. An accurate forecast could lose out to one that can generate and profit from short-term volatility. And because prediction markets are zero-sum, if agents consistently beat unassisted humans, the trading population eventually narrows to agents and insiders.

The success of AI prediction largely hinges on trust, Karger said. Right now, no one knows why model accuracy is improving—or how precise AI forecasting might become. “People don’t trust black boxes to make forecasts,” he added. There’s also a need to improve methodologies. For example, every ForecastBench result currently rests on a yes-or-no question, leaving continuous outcomes and high-value, high-consequence events untouched and unmeasured. The team is working to expand the benchmark to these domains.

Paleka suggests that the solution, at least for now, is to pair human judgment and AI so that each can handle what it does best. Karger sets a higher bar: “If we get to the point where automated forecasts are being used in decision making at companies, policy groups, and the government, it would only be because people trust these models and understand what is happening under the hood.”

Samuel Greengard is an author and journalist based in West Linn, OR, USA.

item.title: When Cybersecurity Decisions Become Physical Safety Decisions
item.dc:creator: Mridul Agrawal
item.description: The most useful measure of cyber-physical resilience is whether an organization can still make safe, informed decisions while some of its digital capabilities are impaired.
item.content:encoded:
In a conventional IT incident, isolating a compromised machine from the network is often a sensible first move. Now imagine that machine is part of the control environment for a hospital’s electrical distribution system or an airport terminal’s power infrastructure. Network isolation might stop unauthorized commands. It might also remove information that operators depend on to manage equipment safely. Whether the equipment itself changes state depends on the system architecture. That uncertainty is the point: a cybersecurity response has become an engineering decision.

In my work designing electrical systems for critical facilities, I have learned to look at two kinds of connections. An electrical one-line diagram shows how power reaches essential loads. A network diagram shows how measurements, commands, and alarms travel between devices. Either drawing may be correct while still leaving out a consequential dependency. The question is not simply whether the network is secure, but what the physical system will do—and what its operators will know—when part of that network becomes unavailable.

Consider a hypothetical campus with two incoming power sources, local protective relays, and a supervisory system that displays breaker positions and supports remote operating procedures. A security team detects suspicious traffic to the supervisory system and isolates its network connection. That may be exactly the right containment action. The protective relays could continue to perform their local functions, and the power supply might remain uninterrupted. Yet operators may lose reliable visibility into equipment status just as they need to decide whether a load transfer is safe. The new risk is not necessarily that isolation trips a breaker. It is that the next human decision is made with incomplete or stale information.

This distinction changes how I think an incident playbook should be written. “Disconnect the affected controller” is a cybersecurity action, not a complete description of a safe operating state. Before an incident, teams should know which functions merely display information, which can issue control commands, which protections operate independently, and how equipment behaves when communications fail. They should also agree on how to verify the actual equipment state after telemetry has been interrupted. An automatic network response that is appropriate for one device may be inappropriate for another that participates in a time-sensitive physical process.

The need to account for physical consequences is not new NIST’s Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security explicitly addresses the performance, reliability, and safety requirements of systems that interact with the physical world. Its newer incident-response guidance also places response and recovery within a broader risk-management process. What these principles demand in practice is cooperation across a boundary that organizations often maintain for good reasons: security professionals understand the threat and containment options; operating teams understand the process; and engineers understand how the electrical equipment and its safeguards are intended to behave. A sound decision needs all three perspectives.

I would therefore design incident responses around pre-agreed operating conditions rather than a single instruction to isolate or shut down. Depending on the facility, these might include continued operation with closely monitored, restricted access; loss of supervisory connectivity while verified local protections remain active; or a controlled transition to an engineered safe state. These are not universal recipes. Each condition needs site-specific hazard analysis, assigned decision authority, and a clear route back to normal operation. Sometimes prompt isolation is the safest choice. Sometimes containment must be coordinated with operations to avoid creating a second emergency.

One useful test is a joint exercise that begins after the intrusion has already been detected. Suppose the engineering workstation is unavailable, several status indications are stale, and the facility must perform a scheduled electrical transfer. Who can authorize the next action? Which independent indications can confirm the position of the equipment? Can the planned transfer be postponed without compromising essential service? What evidence is required before the isolated system can be reconnected? Those questions expose weaknesses that a network-only penetration test or an electrical-only commissioning exercise may miss. An accurate inventory of both digital assets and their operating roles is a prerequisite.

Computing professionals have an important role in making those decisions less fragile. Interfaces can distinguish live measurements from last-known values. Control systems can separate monitoring privileges from switching authority, make commands traceable, and communicate the consequences of a lost connection. Recovery workflows can require evidence that both software integrity and physical operating conditions have been restored. None of these features substitutes for independent protection, interlocking, trained operators, or sound engineering. They make it less likely that a security team and an operations team will act on different understandings of the same system.

I believe the most useful measure of cyber-physical resilience is not simply whether a system blocks an attacker or stays online. It is whether the organization can still make safe, informed decisions while some of its digital capabilities are impaired. In a critical facility, disconnecting a device changes more than a network diagram. It may change what the people responsible for the physical system can see, verify, and control. That is why cybersecurity response and physical-system safety must be designed together—before either team is making decisions under pressure.

His work focuses on infrastructure reliability, operational resilience, and the intersection of cybersecurity, operational technology, and physical safety.
